The Arabs used to do this: when a daughter was born to one of them and he kept her alive, he would dress her in a woollen or hair garment and leave her to graze the camels and sheep. *Among us is the one who prevented the burying women, and gave life to the buried girl, so she was not buried.*

(p-434) ﴿And when the scrolls are unrolled﴾. The scrolls of deeds were folded up over the deeds, and they will be unrolled on the Day of Resurrection so that every person may read his book. It is said: the scrolls that fly out into the right hands and the left hands are for the recompense, and they are scrolls other than the scrolls of deeds. Abu Raja', Qatadah, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Shaybah, Abu Ja'far, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "nushirat" (نُشِرَتْ) with a light shin, and the rest of the seven read it with a doubled shin (نُشِّرَتْ). Kashṭ (كَشْط) of the sky means folding it up, like the folding of the scroll (السِّجِلّ). It is also said: it is removed, as the skin is stripped (يُكْشَطُ) from the sacrificed animal. 'Abdullah read "qushitat" (قُشِطَتْ) with a qaf, and these two (kashṭ and qashṭ) frequently alternate, as in their saying: "'arabī quḥḥ" and "kuḥḥ", and his reading "qāfūran" was mentioned earlier, meaning "kāfūran". Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read "su'‘‘irat" (سُعِّرَتْ) with a doubled 'ayn, and the rest of the seven read it with a light 'ayn; this is also the reading of 'Ali. Qatadah said: the anger of God the Exalted and the sins of the children of Adam kindled it. The answer to "idha" and what is joined to it is "﻿ʿalimat nafsun mā aḥḍarat﻿" (﴿every soul will know what it has brought forward﴾). "Nafs" here is generalising in affirmative speech in meaning: what it has brought forward of good by which it enters Paradise, or of evil by which it enters the Fire. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the singular was used to draw attention to the insignificance of the single human being and the weakness of his defence of himself. End of quotation.

This surah was recited in the presence of 'Abdullah, and when the reader reached ﴿every soul will know what it has brought forward﴾, 'Abdullah said: "and its back was broken" (wa-nqaṭa'a ẓahruhā).

(bi-l-khunnas) The majority said: the seven planets: the Sun, the Moon, Saturn, Mercury, Mars, Venus and Jupiter. 'Ali said: the five apart from the Sun and the Moon; the five run with the Sun and the Moon, and they retreat until they are hidden by the light of the Sun. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: they recede (takhnisu) in their course, which is observed by sight, and they are "jawārin" in the sky, and they hide (yaknisu) in their zodiac signs, that is, they conceal themselves. 'Ali also said, along with al-Hasan and Qatadah: they are all the stars, because they recede and hide by day when they disappear. Al-Zamakhshari said: they recede by day and hide by night, that is, they rise in their places like wild beasts in their lairs. End of quotation. 'Abdullah, al-Nakha'i, Jabir ibn Zayd and a group said: what is meant by ﴿al-khunnas﴾ and ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾ is the wild cattle, because they perform these actions in their hiding places (kanā'is). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: they are gazelles, and "khunnas" is an attribute of the wild cows (anūq), because they are characterised by khans (recoiling). Likewise the wild cattle.

(ʿas'asa) in the dialect of Quraysh (meaning it turned away / began to recede). Al-Hasan said: its darkness came on, and this is preferred because it is contrasted with His saying: ﴿and the morning when it breathes﴾. So these are two states. Al-Mubarrad said: He swore by its coming and its going. Its breathing: that it comes with it refreshment and a breeze, so it is as if it were a breath for it, metaphorically.

(innahu) that is, indeed this about which the oath is sworn, that is, indeed the Qur'an, ﴿is the word of a noble messenger﴾. The majority: that he is Gabriel, peace be upon him. It is said: Muhammad (ﷺ). "Karīm" is an attribute that requires the negation of all blemishes and the affirmation of the attributes of praise fitting to him.

﴿Possessor of power﴾, like His saying: ﴿mighty in strength﴾ [al-Najm: 5].

﴿With the Lord of the Throne﴾: the standing (kaynūna) befitting the honour of rank and the greatness of station. It is said: "al-'arsh" is connected to "makīn" (established), obeyed. Then an indication to ﴿with the Lord of the Throne﴾, that is, he is obeyed among the close angels of God, who act upon his command. Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywah, Abu al-Barahsam and Ibn Miqsam read "thumma" with a damma on the tha', as a conjunction (of sequence). The majority read "thamma" with a fatha, an adverb of place for the distant. Al-Zamakhshari said: it was read "thumma", to exalt the trustworthiness and to show that it is the best of his counted attributes. End of quotation. The author of al-Lawami' said: it means "obeyed and trustworthy", and "thumma" came to mean "wa" (and) after its convention for sequence and delay as a conjunction; this is because Gabriel, peace be upon him, possessed both attributes together in one state, so if someone went to the sequence and delay in this conjunction, meaning "obeyed among the exalted assembly, then trustworthy when separated from them at the time of his revelation to the prophets, peace be upon them", it would be permissible were a report to be transmitted about it. End of quotation. (Amin) worthy of being accepted in speech, so that what he says is believed, entrusted with what is sent of revelation and the carrying out of command.

﴿Your companion is not mad﴾: He negated what they used to attribute to him and falsely accused him of, namely madness.

﴿And he certainly saw him﴾, that is, the Messenger (ﷺ) saw Gabriel, peace be upon him. This vision was after the matter of the cave of Hira, when he saw him on a chair between the heaven and the earth, in his form, having six hundred wings. It is said: it is the vision in which he saw him at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha), and that place was called "horizon" metaphorically. He had another vision in Medina, but this is not it. The horizon was described as "clear" because it was narrated that it was in the east, from where the sun rises, said by Qatadah and Sufyan; and also every horizon is in complete clarity. It is said: on the western horizon of the sky, related by Ibn Shajarah. Mujahid said: he saw him toward the Jiyad, which is the east of Mecca. Ibn Mas'ud? (no) — ʿAbdullah, Ibn ʿAbbas, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn al-Zubayr, ʿA'ishah, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, Ibn Jubayr, ʿUrwah, Hisham ibn Jundub, Mujahid and others read "bi-ẓanīn" with a ẓa (ظ), meaning "accused"; and from the seven, the two Nahwiyyun (al-Kisa'i and Hamzah? — per the text: the two grammarians) and Ibn Kathir: this is the counterpart of the earlier description "amin". It is said: its meaning is "weak in strength to convey", from their saying "a ẓanūn well", when it has little water. It is likewise with ẓa in the codex of ʿAbdullah. ʿUthman, Ibn ʿAbbas also, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and a group besides them, and the rest of the seven, read it with a ḍād, meaning "miserly": one who withholds it, does not convey what he is told, and is stingy, as the soothsayer does until his fee is given. Al-Tabari said: the codices of all the Qur'an-copies are with ḍād.

﴿And it is not the word of an accursed Satan﴾, that is, the one who appears to him is an angel, not like the one who appears to the soothsayers.

﴿Where then are you going?﴾ A reproach to them, since they attributed him once to madness, once to soothsaying, and once to other things from which he is innocent. Al-Zamakhshari said: as one says to someone who leaves the highway, straying or going off onto the byways of the path: "Where are you going?" Their condition was likened to his condition in abandoning the truth and turning from it to falsehood. End of quotation.

(dhikr) admonition and advice. ﴿For whoever wills﴾ is a substitute for "lil-'alamin". Then He linked the will of the servants to the will of God the Exalted. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: then God the Exalted specified "whoever wills uprightness" by mention, honouring and alerting, and as a mention of their engagement in deeds of uprightness; then He explained that the servant's acquisition in general, in uprightness and otherwise, occurs only with God's creation and His bringing about faith in the breast of a person. End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari said: they were substituted for them because those who willed uprightness by entering Islam are the ones who benefit from the admonition, as if it were not addressed to others, though all are addressed.

﴿And you will not will﴾ uprightness, O you who wish it, except by the grace of God the Exalted and His kindness; you will not will it, O you who do not wish it, except by God's compulsion and coercion. End of quotation. Thus Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Zamakhshari each explained "will" according to his own school. Al-Hasan said: the Arabs did not will Islam until God willed it for them.

It is likewise with ẓa in the codex of ʿAbdullah. ʿUthman, Ibn ʿAbbas also, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and a group besides them, and the rest of the seven, read it with a ḍād, meaning "miserly": one who withholds it, does not convey what he is told, and is stingy, as the soothsayer does until his fee is given. Al-Tabari said: the codices of all the Qur'an-copies are with ḍād.

﴿And it is not the word of an accursed Satan﴾, that is, the one who appears to him is an angel, not like the one who appears to the soothsayers.

﴿Where then are you going?﴾ A reproach to them, since they attributed him once to madness, once to soothsaying, and once to other things from which he is innocent. Al-Zamakhshari said: as one says to someone who leaves the highway, straying or going off onto the byways of the path: "Where are you going?" Their condition was likened to his condition in abandoning the truth and turning from it to falsehood. End of quotation.

(dhikr) admonition and advice. ﴿For whoever wills﴾ is a substitute for "lil-'alamin". Then He linked the will of the servants to the will of God the Exalted. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: then God the Exalted specified "whoever wills uprightness" by mention, honouring and alerting, and as a mention of their engagement in deeds of uprightness; then He explained that the servant's acquisition in general, in uprightness and otherwise, occurs only with God's creation and His bringing about faith in the breast of a person. End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari said: they were substituted for them because those who willed uprightness by entering Islam are the ones who benefit from the admonition, as if it were not addressed to others, though all are addressed.

﴿And you will not will﴾ uprightness, O you who wish it, except by the grace of God the Exalted and His kindness; you will not will it, O you who do not wish it, except by God's compulsion and coercion. End of quotation. Thus Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Zamakhshari each explained "will" according to his own school. Al-Hasan said: the Arabs did not will Islam until God willed it for them.

(p-434) ﴿And when the scrolls are unrolled﴾. The scrolls of deeds were folded up over the deeds, and they will be unrolled on the Day of Resurrection so that every person may read his book. It is said: the scrolls that fly out into the right hands and the left hands are for the recompense, and they are scrolls other than the scrolls of deeds. Abu Raja', Qatadah, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Shaybah, Abu Ja'far, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "nushirat" (نُشِرَتْ) with a light shin, and the rest of the seven read it with a doubled shin (نُشِّرَتْ). Kashṭ (كَشْط) of the sky means folding it up, like the folding of the scroll (السِّجِلّ). It is also said: it is removed, as the skin is stripped (يُكْشَطُ) from the sacrificed animal. 'Abdullah read "qushitat" (قُشِطَتْ) with a qaf, and these two (kashṭ and qashṭ) frequently alternate, as in their saying: "'arabī quḥḥ" and "kuḥḥ", and his reading "qāfūran" was mentioned earlier, meaning "kāfūran". Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read "su'‘‘irat" (سُعِّرَتْ) with a doubled 'ayn, and the rest of the seven read it with a light 'ayn; this is also the reading of 'Ali. Qatadah said: the anger of God the Exalted and the sins of the children of Adam kindled it. The answer to "idha" and what is joined to it is "﻿ʿalimat nafsun mā aḥḍarat﻿" (﴿every soul will know what it has brought forward﴾). "Nafs" here is generalising in affirmative speech in meaning: what it has brought forward of good by which it enters Paradise, or of evil by which it enters the Fire. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the singular was used to draw attention to the insignificance of the single human being and the weakness of his defence of himself. End of quotation.

This surah was recited in the presence of 'Abdullah, and when the reader reached ﴿every soul will know what it has brought forward﴾, 'Abdullah said: "and its back was broken" (wa-nqaṭa'a ẓahruhā).

(bi-l-khunnas) The majority said: the seven planets: the Sun, the Moon, Saturn, Mercury, Mars, Venus and Jupiter. 'Ali said: the five apart from the Sun and the Moon; the five run with the Sun and the Moon, and they retreat until they are hidden by the light of the Sun. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: they recede (takhnisu) in their course, which is observed by sight, and they are "jawārin" in the sky, and they hide (yaknisu) in their zodiac signs, that is, they conceal themselves. 'Ali also said, along with al-Hasan and Qatadah: they are all the stars, because they recede and hide by day when they disappear. Al-Zamakhshari said: they recede by day and hide by night, that is, they rise in their places like wild beasts in their lairs. End of quotation. 'Abdullah, al-Nakha'i, Jabir ibn Zayd and a group said: what is meant by ﴿al-khunnas﴾ and ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾ is the wild cattle, because they perform these actions in their hiding places (kanā'is). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: they are gazelles, and "khunnas" is an attribute of the wild cows (anūq), because they are characterised by khans (recoiling). Likewise the wild cattle.

(ʿas'asa) in the dialect of Quraysh (meaning it turned away / began to recede). Al-Hasan said: its darkness came on, and this is preferred because it is contrasted with His saying: ﴿and the morning when it breathes﴾. So these are two states. Al-Mubarrad said: He swore by its coming and its going. Its breathing: that it comes with it refreshment and a breeze, so it is as if it were a breath for it, metaphorically.

(innahu) that is, indeed this about which the oath is sworn, that is, indeed the Qur'an, ﴿is the word of a noble messenger﴾. The majority: that he is Gabriel, peace be upon him. It is said: Muhammad (ﷺ). "Karīm" is an attribute that requires the negation of all blemishes and the affirmation of the attributes of praise fitting to him.

﴿Possessor of power﴾, like His saying: ﴿mighty in strength﴾ [al-Najm: 5].

﴿With the Lord of the Throne﴾: the standing (kaynūna) befitting the honour of rank and the greatness of station. It is said: "al-'arsh" is connected to "makīn" (established), obeyed. Then an indication to ﴿with the Lord of the Throne﴾, that is, he is obeyed among the close angels of God, who act upon his command. Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywah, Abu al-Barahsam and Ibn Miqsam read "thumma" with a damma on the tha', as a conjunction (of sequence). The majority read "thamma" with a fatha, an adverb of place for the distant. Al-Zamakhshari said: it was read "thumma", to exalt the trustworthiness and to show that it is the best of his counted attributes. End of quotation. The author of al-Lawami' said: it means "obeyed and trustworthy", and "thumma" came to mean "wa" (and) after its convention for sequence and delay as a conjunction; this is because Gabriel, peace be upon him, possessed both attributes together in one state, so if someone went to the sequence and delay in this conjunction, meaning "obeyed among the exalted assembly, then trustworthy when separated from them at the time of his revelation to the prophets, peace be upon them", it would be permissible were a report to be transmitted about it. End of quotation. (Amin) worthy of being accepted in speech, so that what he says is believed, entrusted with what is sent of revelation and the carrying out of command.

﴿Your companion is not mad﴾: He negated what they used to attribute to him and falsely accused him of, namely madness.

﴿And he certainly saw him﴾, that is, the Messenger (ﷺ) saw Gabriel, peace be upon him. This vision was after the matter of the cave of Hira, when he saw him on a chair between the heaven and the earth, in his form, having six hundred wings. It is said: it is the vision in which he saw him at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha), and that place was called "horizon" metaphorically. He had another vision in Medina, but this is not it. The horizon was described as "clear" because it was narrated that it was in the east, from where the sun rises, said by Qatadah and Sufyan; and also every horizon is in complete clarity. It is said: on the western horizon of the sky, related by Ibn Shajarah. Mujahid said: he saw him toward the Jiyad, which is the east of Mecca. Ibn Mas'ud?
